title: Beef Tataki
subtitle: Seared and sliced beef with soy and ginger dressing
excerpt: Tataki is defined by the contrast between the seared, almost charred exterior and the raw centre. The beef goes into a very hot pan for about 90 seconds per side -- no more. It is then chilled before slicing so it holds its shape cleanly. Buy the best sirloin you can find.
sourceNotes: Tataki is a Japanese preparation in which fish or beef is briefly seared at high heat and then sliced thin, served with a ponzu or soy dressing. The technique originated in Tosa province, now Kochi Prefecture, and is most traditionally associated with bonito fish.

content.text: Chill the beef after searing and before slicing -- room-temperature beef will compress and tear rather than cut cleanly into thin rounds. Thirty minutes in the freezer works well.

items.prepNote: centre-cut piece, sinew trimmed, tied into a neat log with kitchen string

content.text: Mix the soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, and grated ginger together to make the dressing. Set aside.
Pat the beef dry and season with salt. Heat the sunflower oil in the frying pan over the highest heat possible until just smoking.

Sear the beef for 90 seconds per side (about 6 minutes total for the whole log, rotating every 90 seconds) so the outside is deeply coloured and the centre is still raw. Remove and wrap tightly in cling film to shape, then refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Unwrap the beef and slice very thinly -- about 3 mm -- with the sharpest knife you have.
Arrange the slices on a cold plate, overlapping slightly. Spoon the dressing over the top and scatter with the sliced spring onion.

items.cause: Not chilled long enough after searing.
items.fix: Return to the freezer for another 15-20 minutes. The beef should feel firm to the touch, not soft.

items.cause: Pan not hot enough or beef too wet.
items.fix: Pat the beef completely dry and make sure the pan is smoking before the beef goes in.
